Therapy approaches | Play therapy

When play helps a child show what words cannot yet hold.

Understand the difference between therapeutic play and ordinary recreation, how caregivers may be involved, and why training and development matter when choosing play therapy.

The idea to keep in mind

Play is a medium, not a diagnosis.

A child can use play to communicate, experiment, and relate. One game, drawing, or toy choice does not establish what the child is feeling or what has happened to them.

Understanding the approach

The relationship and the purpose make it therapy.

The Association for Play Therapy describes play therapy as the use of a theoretical model and an interpersonal process by a trained therapist to help clients address difficulties through play. The presence of toys alone does not make an activity play therapy. A clinician's decisions, relationship with the child, and clinical purpose distinguish the work from entertainment.

Play can give children ways to express experiences, explore choices, and engage with another person without relying only on adult-style conversation. The therapist attends to the process over time, in developmental and family context. It is not a system for decoding a toy or drawing into a certain hidden meaning.

There are multiple play-therapy approaches. Some involve more therapist direction or a particular goal; others give the child more freedom to lead within clear limits. Child-centered play therapy is one defined relationship-based approach. Ask which model a clinician uses, which ages they work with, and how they include caregivers.

Sources play ccpt psychotherapy

In plain language

A session can be purposeful without looking like a lesson.

A child may be practicing choices, expression, or a relationship rather than producing a worksheet. Progress still needs a thoughtful way of being understood and reviewed.

Inside the work

A first conversation includes the adults as well as the play.

01

Understand the concern

The clinician gathers developmental, family, school, and practical context as appropriate. A single description rarely tells the whole story.

02

Explain the arrangement

Discuss who attends, the model, consent and privacy, caregiver contact, and the intended goals.

03

Develop the work

Sessions build a therapeutic relationship through play and any other agreed elements. The approach should remain responsive to the child.

04

Review outside the room

Discuss changes in daily functioning and the caregiver's observations alongside the therapist's assessment. Adapt or refer when needed.

Sources play ccpt psychotherapy

A worked example

A tower falls. The important moment is what happens next.

A fictional illustration of a play interaction, not an interpretation of any real child.

Fictional teaching example. Not a diagnosis, a client story, or an assigned exercise.

01

The activity

A child builds a tower that collapses. They push the pieces aside and say the game is stupid.

02

The adult response

The therapist notices the frustration and responds without ridicule or rushing to make the tower perfect. They maintain the agreed safety limits.

03

The opening

Depending on the model and the child, the moment might allow expression, trying another choice, asking for help, or tolerating an imperfect outcome. It is not proof of a particular disorder.

Why not simply teach the child the right answer?

Different models use direction differently. A therapist may support a child's own problem-solving or introduce a specific skill when appropriate. Either way, the response should fit the therapeutic plan, development, and relationship rather than simply reward compliance.

The tower is not important because it symbolizes a single correct explanation. The child's experience in the interaction, and how this fits with concerns outside the room, gives the clinician more useful information over time.

Sources play ccpt psychotherapy

Go a little deeper

What to look for beyond the toys.

A caregiver should be able to understand the approach even when private session details are not shared.

01A defined modelAsk how the clinician makes decisions.Read more +

Play therapy includes a range of approaches. The therapist should describe the model, their relevant preparation, and why they believe it fits the child and the concerns presented.

A cheerful play space is not evidence of specialized training or a complete treatment plan.

02Developmental fitThe activity should fit the child, not an assumed age stereotype.Read more +

Language, attention, sensory preferences, culture, disability, and relationship experiences can affect how a child participates. A therapist can adapt materials and pacing rather than assume every child enjoys the same kinds of play.

Ask about the clinician's age range and experience with needs relevant to your child.

03Caregiver partnershipHome context remains important.Read more +

Caregivers may provide information, receive consultation, or participate in selected work, depending on the model and plan. Clarify how communication and confidentiality work before treatment begins.

A therapist can discuss themes and progress without turning every private play moment into a report card.

04Safety and limitsFreedom to play does not mean freedom to harm.Read more +

Clear limits can protect the child, therapist, and materials while preserving a respectful relationship. Boundaries are part of the therapeutic setting.

The caregiver and therapist should also discuss how safety concerns or important new information will be handled.

Sources play ccpt psychotherapy

Fit, choice and limitations

Neither a shortcut to certainty nor just supervised recreation.

Interpretation needs humility

It is inappropriate to infer abuse, a diagnosis, or a family fact from one toy choice or drawing. Concerns need careful assessment and appropriate procedures rather than symbolic certainty.

The right service needs confirmation

A clinician who sees children does not automatically offer a particular play-therapy model or credential. This educational guide does not establish current M.F.T. availability.

Sources play ccpt psychotherapy

Your questions, answered

More to know before choosing.

Will my child talk about the problem directly?

They may, but play can be the main medium. The therapist should not force a child to narrate difficult experiences simply to make the session look more like adult therapy.

How will I know whether it is helping?

Ask how the clinician will review the agreed goals, functioning, and caregiver observations. A satisfying play session alone is not the only measure, and a difficult session is not automatically failure.

Will I stay in the room?

That depends on the model, the child's needs, and the treatment agreement. Confirm the plan rather than assuming either constant participation or complete exclusion.

Is every therapist who has toys a play therapist?

No. Training, theoretical approach, and scope matter. Ask directly about relevant education and credentials rather than inferring them from room materials.

How is child-centered play therapy different?

It is a specific relationship-based approach in which the child generally leads the play within therapeutic limits. The child-centered guide explains that distinction in more detail.

For practical questions, contact the support team. Please keep clinical details out of the initial email.
